title: Parliaments
objective: After this level you can explain how parliaments work.
summary: A parliament is a place for talking that makes laws, controls taxes and holds government to account. Iceland's Althing (about 930) has one chamber; the UK's Parliament has two.

cards.headline: Iceland's Althing met at the same site for more than eight centuries.
cards.body: Iceland's Althing was founded at Thingvellir around 930 and met there until 1798. Britannica counts it among the oldest national parliaments in the world. So what exactly is a parliament for? The name gives the first clue.

cards.headline: A place for talking
cards.body: Parliament comes from the Old French parlement, "a speaking, talk", from parler, "to speak". That's the core of it: a room (or, in Iceland's case, a site) where a country's representatives argue things out in the open before anything is decided. Kings could simply give orders; a parliament has to talk things through first.

cards.headline: Laws, money, scrutiny
cards.body: Take the UK Parliament. Its main job is making laws. Its elected House of Commons has the sole right to impose taxes and decide funding for government services: Level 22's "no tax without consent", now given by elected members. And a prime minister must keep a Commons majority to stay in office, so the government's decisions face constant scrutiny and debate.

mascot.line: Make the laws, hold the purse, question the government. That's the job description.

points: UK: the elected House of Commons

questions.prompt: The name "parliament" grew from which Old French verb, and what did it mean?

options.label: Parer: to protect
options.rationale: Parliament's root is about speaking, not protecting.

options.label: Partir: to divide
options.rationale: Dividing isn't the root; talking is.

options.label: Payer: to pay
options.rationale: Parliaments do handle money, but the root means to speak.

questions.explanation: Parliament comes from Old French parlement, "a speaking, talk", from parler, "to speak".

questions.prompt: Why must a UK prime minister pay close attention to the House of Commons?

options.label: The Commons chooses the monarch
options.rationale: The Commons doesn't choose the monarch.

options.label: The Commons writes every court verdict
options.rationale: Courts, not the Commons, give verdicts.

options.label: They need a Commons majority to stay in office
The Commons sets the prime minister's salary alone
options.rationale: That's not the reason given here.

questions.explanation: A UK prime minister must keep the support of a majority in the House of Commons to remain in office.

questions.prompt: How does the House of Commons' sole right to impose taxes echo Magna Carta's clause 12?

options.label: Both let the king tax whenever he likes
options.rationale: Both do the opposite: they limit who can impose taxes.

options.label: Both abolish taxes altogether
options.rationale: Neither abolishes taxes; both require consent.

options.label: Both make taxes voluntary for each person
options.rationale: Taxes stay compulsory; consent comes first.

options.label: Both require consent before taxes are raised

questions.explanation: Clause 12 required the kingdom's general consent for scutage and aid; today elected Commons members give that consent.
